John Latimer and Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau 



PRIME MINISTER PREMIER MINISTRC 

"Of all the changes which will come 
to Canada in the next generation, 
therefore, we must prevent, surely, 
any of a sort which will diminish 
the essential beauty and lonely 
nature of this country. For if 
that beauty is lost, or if that 
wilderness escapes, the very nature 
and character of this land will have 
passed beyond our grasp. Denied 
an opportunity to breathe the brisk 
freshness of an Atlantic gale, to 
view the unbelievable glory of a 
prairie sunset, to feel the over¬ 
whelming silence of a northern lake, 
we would no longer be Canadians. 

Our lives as individuals would have 
suffered grievously." 

The Canadian Camping Association, 
and the almost half million young 
Canadians who participate in organized 
camping activities each year, share my 
sentiments, I am sure. 

May camping experiences in 1972 
be more inspiring and more exciting than 
ever and may National Camping Day on 
July 19th be a great success. 

To the readers of Ca mpi ng Magazine 
I send my best wishes-; ) 


Pierre Elliott Trudeau 


Ottawa ,

NATIONAL CAMPING DAY 1972 

by Doug Dent, Chairman 
C.C.A. National Camping Day Committee 
145 Lincoln Road 
Waterloo, Ontario 


A general outline of the past his¬ 
tory of National Camping Day 
might be of interest at this point. 
A year ago, this committee was 
created to organize, on a national 
scale, a method of recognizing chil¬ 
dren's camping. Prior to this, 1967 
was the biggest attempt by the 
C.C.A. to celebrate National Camp¬ 
ing Day. 1968 witnessed the postal 
strike which basically curtailed the 
programme with no subsequent ef¬ 
fort in 1969. Prior to Centennial, 
1957 and ’58 I believe, witnessed 
Canadian Camp Week which, how¬ 
ever, posed certain problems re¬ 
sulting in that committee’s recom¬ 
mendation to drop the efTort. 

In 1971 the climax of the Day 
was simultaneous recognition (in 
time zones) by the singing of 
“Taps.” Although short notice was 
given and, in many instances, 
camps received no or too little in¬ 
formation the attempt was success¬ 
ful in reinstituting an annual rec¬ 
ognition. 

The format and objectives of Na¬ 
tional Camping Day were presented 
in the last issue of Canadian Camp¬ 
ing, but should any camps have 
queries, most Provincial Offices 
have Co-ordinators to supply infor¬ 
mation, or such may be obtained 
through this office. 

At this time let’s look at a pos¬ 
sible sequence of events for July 
19th 

— a campfire programme leading 
up to 9 p.m. Daylight Saving Pacific 
time, (etc.), including a talk re: 
what is happening and why, 

— 9 p.m. (etc.) sharp — shoot a 
flaming arrow northward, 

— the camp then circles the fire 
joining hands for “Taps’’, 

— a torchlight parade to the flag¬ 
pole for flag lowering possibility 


with the camp bell tolling, 

— illuminate the flag with a cou¬ 
ple of strong flashlights while “My 
Country is My Cathedral” is sung 
(remember the lowering is slow in 
time with the song), 

— torchlight parade to cabins or 
end with fireworks, 

— NOTE: if generators or elec¬ 
tric power exist, these should be 
shut of! so as not to detract from 
the setting. 

As for flaming arrows! Pick a 
long arrow from your archery 
equipment that is in good condi¬ 
tion; bind burlap or cloth on 
tightly to the tip (3" swath of 
about 10" long) with fine wire; 
soak the end in coal oil, kerosene 
or stove oil (i.e. just the binding) 
for a few hours before use (not 60 
seconds ahead of time in gaso¬ 
line!) ; when ready to light make 
sure the tip is not dripping fluid 
and the shaft is wiped clean; fit the 
arrow to the bow and then light; 
aim the arrow at an angle danger¬ 
ous to neither the archer nor any¬ 
one else. A few other points: don’t 
over weight the tip; the archer’s 
hands should be clean of the fluid 
used; determine the firing area 
ahead of time and have water, 
whatever, available at the expected 
landing site — better still if you can 
fire towards a body of water (but 
make sure the arrow is out); pick 
an archer who will fulfill that re¬ 
sponsibility as is required — pos¬ 
sibly an award to a senior camper. 

The songs are as follows: 

TAPS 

“Day is done 

Gone the Sun 

From the lakes, from the hills, 
from the sky, 

All is well safely rest 

God is nigh.” 


MY COUNTRY IS MY 
CATHEDRAL 

“Side by side and step by step 
Our fathers were marching along 
They were building a road to 
the future 

With a spade and a smile and a 
song 

Out of the wildness and out of 
the woods 

Grew the land that we live in to¬ 
day 

Though the job to be done has 
barely begun 

Here is one thing I’m proud to 
say: 

My country is my Cathedral. 
The northern sky its dome. 
They all call it Canada 
But I call it home. 

The mountains, the lakes, the 
valleys, 

Are friends I have known. 

They call it Canada 
But 1 call it home. 

From the Atlantic to the Pacific 
From the Pole to the U.S.A. 
We’re one united brotherhood 
And united we will stay. 

The people beyond our borders 
And far across the loam, 

They all call it Canada 
But I call it home!” 

Your Provincial Co-ordinator has 
the music to the above song. If you 
need it or any question answered 
please contact your President and 
your enquiry will be handled by 
the Co-ordinator. 

Prime Minister Trudeau will 
proclaim National Camping Day 
this year but all hinges on us. If 
the camps come through, then in 
reality will ’72 be a year to re¬ 
member when literally thousands 
upon thousands of campers cele-

TREMBLAY CANOES 



The finest canoes made in Canada today — correctly designed by craftsmen with 60 years experience for men who 
really know canoes — stable, seaworthy, safe, capable of riding the roughest water or fast water. 

The unsinkable cedar canoes with no space taken up by flotation tanks. 

Tremblay canoes have for the past 7 years been covered with "Verolite", a plastic-coated canvas which ELIMINATES 
ALL EXTERIOR MAINTENANCE. Lighter than painted canvas and far more durable and scuff resistant — not 
affected by heat or cold. 

Seven years use by more than 60 Boys' and Girls' Camps, by Ontario Provincial Police, the Ontario Dept, of Lands & 
Forests and the Dept, of Mines also the Quebec Dept, of Natural Resources also by Lumber and Pulp Companies in 
their spring drives and by Mining & Oil Development Companies and by thousands of canoeists comprising the gen¬ 
eral public has proven that Verolite stands up to the most rigorous demands. 

In the construction of Tremblay Canoes only No. 1 Eastern Canada Cedar is used and only solid Brass nails and Brass 
screws are used. The deck pieces, thwarts and seats are of white Birch. Seats may be either slat style or rawhide 
laced. The interior is finished with Urethane Lacquer to provide years of protection. 

For the fisherman, hunter or camp operator, Tremblay offers a complete range of pointed, V-Stern, or flat-wide 
stern canoes in 38 sizes and models. 

Verolite is now available in red, green or orange. For those who wish canoes of other colours, we still make the 
standard painted canvas canoes. 

Carrying yokes can be built in or provided separately. These are extra. 

Verolite covered canoes do not require periodic painting, thus they do not take on added weight with the passing years. 
Eyery year the demand for Tremblay canoes increases remarkably. 

A Cedar canoe is always preferred by the experienced knowledgeable canoeist. They ride right and handle right. 
For complete information write to the Canadian Sales Representative.

THE SUMMER CAMP EXPERIENCE — 
ONE MOTHER’S VIEWPOINT 


Our four sons have all been sum¬ 
mer campers, and one a counsellor, 
but it wasn’t until the youngest boy 
had departed for camp the last 
summer that I really had time to 
ponder the question, “Just what is 
the most important thing that we 
hope our boys have gained from 
this experience?” 

After the traumatic days of shop¬ 
ping from a lengthy list, label sew¬ 
ing and last-minute laundry, I was 
enjoying the blissful respite from 
parental responsibility that most 
mothers, if they are honest, will ad¬ 
mit is one of their most important 
gains — and after careful thought, 1 
came up with the following. 

Of course, all parents want, and 
perhaps tend to take for granted, 
the more obvious advantages of 
summer camp — fresh air, plenty of 
exercise, good food, safety, adequate 
rest, good counsellors and enough 
of them, a stimulating programme 
and so on. These all play their part 
in giving the youngsters an enjoy¬ 
able and beneficial summer. Rut I 
think the following anecdote best 
illustrates what 1 finally concluded 
was the most important benefit of 
all. 

Some years ago, 1 listened to an 
address by the late Dr. Hi neks, 
founder and at that time head of 
the Toronto Mental Health Asso¬ 
ciation. One particular story made 
a deep impression on me. Dr. 
Hincks told of a young lad, shy, 
inarticulate, completely unskilled 
at athletics and completely ignored 
by his schoolmates. The lonely boy 
spent all his time at recess riding 
around the outskirts of the school 
grounds on his bicycle, trying to* 
see how slowly he could ride with¬ 
out falling off. As he had nothing 


by Dorothy Sims Attfield 


better to do and lacked the initia¬ 
tive to try and break into a group, 
he became very skilled at this. One 
day a wise and concerned teacher, 
who was perceptive enough to 
realize that the boy badly needed 
help, got an inspiration. School 
sports day was approaching, with 
the usual keen rivalry between 
classes for winning points. The 
teacher announced a new kind of 
contest for the great day — a slow 
bicycle race! No need to say who 
won it, to the surprise and delight 
of his classmates — and far more 
important, how it marked the be¬ 
ginning of his acceptance by the 
group. “1 know this story well” 
concluded Dr. Hincks, “because I 
was that boy, and this episode 
marked the turning point in my life 
and the beginning of my lifelong 
interest in mental health work.” 

Of course, what the lad had 
gained was the most important 
thing of all — self-confidence. And 
as confidence spreads rapidly from 
one area to another, it wasn’t long 
before he was improving all around. 

And so I feel most strongly that 
increased confidence is what I want 
our boys to gain from their camp 
experience. 

Naturally, I am not presumptu¬ 
ous enough to try and tell qualified 
and experienced directors and 
counsellors how they should go 
about trying to achieve this, nor 
would it be possible to list the many 
and varied ways limited only by the 
imagination. But from a mother’s 
many years of experience around 
youngsters of all ages and types, 
may I suggest that more emphasis 
could perhaps be laid on the follow¬ 
ing points. 


First and foremost, counsellors 
should be chosen as much for their 
perceptual skills, understanding 
and kindness as for the more ob¬ 
vious qualities of leadership and 
physical skills. 

Secondly, counsellors themselves 
could increase their efforts to look 
underneath surface behaviour for 
feelings of inadequacy. What areas 
of participation does a youngster 
avoid — is it because he really has 
no interest in the activities or be¬ 
cause lie feels he cannot “measure 
up”? If the latter is the case, a little 
extra coaching during “free” time 
plus plenty of encouragement and 
emphasis on what he is doing cor¬ 
rectly (not wrongly) can work 
wonders. 

Last but not least, could more 
emphasis lie laid upon improving 
social skills? Athletic prowess is 
important to the youngsters, but a 
big part of their feeling of belong¬ 
ing is social acceptance by the 
group. Perhaps the trouble maker, 
the bully or the chronic “beefer” 
(and there’s usually one in every 
group) could be given more respon¬ 
sibility, not less; for example in 
coaching younger boys at something 
he himself is skilled in doing. As 
well as campfire singsongs, how 
about campfire “talkathons” where 
every child is encouraged to voice 
his opinions, likes, dislikes and even 
fears. As well as helping communi¬ 
cation skills, these sessions could 
provide valuable clues as to areas 
of need in each child. 

But however it is achieved, if my 
child comes home from camp with 
increased self-confidence, the exper¬ 
ience will be an unqualified success 
— for both of us.

Aquatic Danger: Spinal Injuries 


Jocelyn Palm, Executive Secretary Ontario Branch, 
Royal Life Saving Society, Canada. 


Introduction 

Last summer a nineteen-year-old 
boy dove into a swimming pool, hit 
his head and weakly moved his anus 
in order to get back to the surface. 
He was able to formulate groaning 
sounds although he could not form 
words and felt completely ex¬ 
hausted. Friends dragged him from 
the water and took him to hospital 
where he remains today, almost to¬ 
tally paralyzed. 

Injuries to the vertebrae protect¬ 
ing the spinal cord or to the spinal 
cord itself are extremely serious 
because they frequently result in 
paralysis. In one hospital in Tor¬ 
onto 523 cases of paralysis from the 
neck down have been treated prior 
to 1972; 109 of these cases were a 
result of diving accidents.* 

1 he unfortunate fact concerning 
most diving accidents is that these 
are wholly preventable. Diving into 
shallow water, falling while water 
skiing at high speeds and being hit 
by waves close to the shore of surf 
beaches are some of the major 
causes of spinal injuries in aquatic 
sports. Many of these accidents in¬ 
volve good swimmers who are un¬ 
aware of the risks, persons who are 
fooling around and skilled water 
skiers who assume unnecessary risks. 
Types of Injuries 

The spinal cord is a thin cylin¬ 
drical structure protected by a 
series of bony vertebrae to form the 
spinal column. Between each ver¬ 
tebrae is a cartilagenous disc which 
tends to absorb and cushion the 
shock of one vertebrae moving 
against the next as the body moves. 


Injuries to the spine are classified 
as fracture-dislocations, pure frac¬ 
tures or pure dislocations. The 
damage to the vertebrae is repair¬ 
able, however the spinal cord itself 
must be protected from squeezing 
or shearing and this is the key in 
careful handling of spinal accident 
victims. Rarely is the spinal cord 
cut in half at the instant of impact 
but as a result of pressure of broken 
vertebrae on the spinal cord a cer¬ 
tain number of nerve cells are dam¬ 
aged; if this pressure is maintained 
the cells die and cannot be replaced. 
Blood vessels supplying the spinal 
cord itself may be ruptured and re¬ 
lease a volume of fluid which fills 
the very small space between the 
cord and the vertebrae. If the pres¬ 
sure of this fluid builds it com¬ 
pounds the problem. 

Depending upon the level of the 
injury and the extent of the dam¬ 
age, a variety of problems may re¬ 
sult from the impact. If the injury 
is in the first two to three vertebrae, 
there is immediate loss of respira¬ 
tory control. At the level of the 
fifth to seventh vertebrae, a paral¬ 
ysis of the lower limbs and a partial 
loss of power in the arms is evident. 
An injury lower than this may re¬ 
sult in a victim with full movement 
in the arms and a loss of power in 
the lower limbs. Often the impact 
causes a fracture of the vertebrae, 
however it is the mishandling by 
well-intentioned by-standers dis¬ 
placing the fracture which causes 
damage to the spinal cord. 

Recognition 

A rescuer who has seen the acci¬ 
dent occur, or who has had the de¬ 
tails of the accident related to him, 
will regard this information with 
a high index of suspicion — a spinal 
injury is probable. The situations 
in which spinal injuries occur in¬ 
variably involve the striking of the 
normally supple body against some 
immovable force. 


Additional indications of pos¬ 
sible spinal damage are noted in 
the condition of the victim, such as; 
laceration to the head, cessation of 
breathing and inability to move 
legs or arms or both. Occasionally 
the injury may not be obvious. The 
rescuer must suspect spinal injury 
if there is any back deformity, 
bruising over the spinal column, 
weakness or loss of sensation in the 
limbs. 

Procedures for the Rescuer 

Upon recognizing the subject 
with a possible spinal injury, the 
rescuer should immediately sum¬ 
mon the assistance of other persons 
and call for a spineboard or any 
suitable flat, strong and sizeable 
surface upon which the subject may 
ultimately be transported to proper 
medical treatment. 

The early application of the fol¬ 
lowing procedures is emphasized 
for even the slightest suspicion of a 
spinal injury because the onset of 
paralysis may be delayed, leading 
the rescuer into a false sense of 
security concerning the extent of 
the injuries. 

Where the rescuer has seen the 
incident develop and has reason to 
suspect a spinal injury lie will begin 
procedures to immobilize and place 
traction on the spine as early as 
possible. 

If the victim is below the surface 
of the water, the rescuer will surface 
dive, dive, or jump to a point rela¬ 
tively near to the subject. There are 
three traction carries which have 
thus far proven effective in recover¬ 
ing the subject to the surface. 

(i) Approaching from behind the 
subject the rescuer hooks his 
arms under the subject’s arms 
and places his hands against 
either side of the subject’s 
head and over the ears. The 
rescuer exerts an upward 
force on the subject’s head in 
a straight line with the spine. 
The subject’s spine is inimo-

Direct Method and Traction

Three methods of surfacing a subject with a spinal injury

1356 Regina Street, North Bay, Ontario 
Telephone 474-2777 


Manufacturers of 

Trip and Incamp Tents, Flys, Packsacks, Tarps, Sleeping 
Bags, etc.. Made of Nylon, Sail Silk, Fabrine, Cotton, etc. 
Also Foam Mattresses and General Repairs 



10 























bilized against the rescuer's 
upper body. A second rescuer, 
if available, could assist by 
gently pulling at the subject’s 
ankles, again in a straight line 
with the subject’s spine. 

(ii) The single rescuer who is un¬ 
able to reach far enough 
around the subject to grasp 
under his arms may use a dif¬ 
ferent method. Facing the 
subject from the side the res¬ 
cuer places one forearm 
against the subject’s chest 
allowing the subject’s chin to 
rest between his thumb and 
his fingers. The other hand is 
placed firmly at the base of 
the subject’s skull and that 
forearm braced against the 
subject’s back. Pressing up¬ 
ward with both hands, trac¬ 
tion is achieved. Using a con¬ 
tinuous leg kick the rescuer 
transports the subject to the 
surface. 

(iii) Where the single rescuer re¬ 
quires the use of one arm to 
get to the surface, he may 
reach over the subject’s shoul¬ 
der, placing one arm around 
the subject’s head. The palm 
of the hand presses on one 
side of the head while the 
other side is braced against 
the rescuer’s shoulder. By ex¬ 
erting upward pressure the 
rescuer is able to maintain 
some traction and support the 
subject’s back against his 
body. 

At the surface the subject is sup¬ 
ported on his back with firm, steady 
and smooth traction by pulling on 
the feet and head with the trunk 
supported. There should be no 
flexion or rotation of the spine. It 
is obvious that this position can 
only be achieved with a minimum 
of three and preferably five persons. 
The procedure is most efficiently 
accomplished in shallow water 
where rescuers have a firm stance. 
Steps should be taken to move to 
shallow water as early as possible. 

If the subject has stopped breath¬ 
ing Direct Method is initiated as 
early as possible while the traction 
is maintained. No hyperextension 
of the neck is performed. It may be 
necessary to lift the jaw to achieve 
an open airway without hyperex- 
terfsion. 

A subject who, following the ac¬ 


cident, is seen floating on his face 
is most adequately turned onto his 
back by reaching under his arms to 
grasp the head between the rescuer’s 
palms. The rescuer’s body supports 
the back and the forearms are 
pressed against the subject’s chest. 
In rolling over the rescuer rolls 
while submerging himself and turn¬ 
ing the subject onto his back. Once 
the subject is turned the procedures 
which were described earlier are 
initiated (i.e. traction and immo¬ 
bilization) . 

The subject should be placed on 
a spineboard or suitable object as 
early as possible. The board is 
placed under the subject by knifing 
it into the water beside the victim, 
then floating it up into position 
underneath the subject. Traction is 
maintained throughout in addition 
to artificial respiration where neces¬ 
sary. 

Once the subject is on the board, 
the head is supported on both sides 
by rolled wet towels, sand bags or 
other suitable objects. 

NOTE: Caution in gently and 
carefully handling a subject with 
a suspected spinal injury may 
well be repaid in the prevention 
of further injury or consequences 
of paralysis. 

Follow-up Procedure 

Once the spine has been stabil¬ 
ized, (i.e. immobilization and trac¬ 
tion) it is essential that the subject 
be transported to hospital imme¬ 
diately. The subject should be cov¬ 
ered to maintain body temperature. 
Should the trip to hospital be a 
lengthy journey, an additional 
complication may arise from the 
body’s inability to affect heat loss 
through flushing and perspiring be¬ 
low the level of the injury. In these 
cases the victim’s temperature may 
rise to dangerously high levels and 
supplementary procedures to lower 
the temperature may be necessary 
if the victim is to survive, e.g. al¬ 
cohol sponge. Any delay in seeking 
medical help increases the risk of 
unfortunate consequences and fur¬ 
ther irreversible damage. 

Any indication or possibility of 
spinal damage should be followed 
up with a medical examination in 
order to eliminate the need for 
concern or to ensure prompt and 
correct treatment. 

Prevention 

Every person with a responsibil¬ 


ity for aquatic sports must do every¬ 
thing possible to prevent spinal 
injuries. Water depths should be 
labelled in swimming pools and on 
waterfronts. Diving boards should 
be securely mounted and placed to 
provide a minimum depth of 9 feet 
for a one metre board, 12 feet for a 
five metre and 15 feet for ten 
metres. Adequate unobstructed 
headroom must also be provided 
around the diving board. Under¬ 
water hazards, e.g. cribs, rocks, 
shoals, etc. should be marked. 
Horseplay and fooling should be 
stopped before an accident devel¬ 
ops. Water skiing and boating 
should be supervised in order to 
avoid the possibility of accidents. 
Swimming areas in lakes and rivers 
should be marked to warn boaters 
to stay clear. Skin and scuba divers 
must display a diver’s flog (red 
square with diagonal white stripe) 
to warn boaters to remain at least 
100 feet clear. 

Practice in the correct procedures 
for dealing with spinal injuries 
should be included in the training 
of camp leaders and staff along with 
the routine practice in resuscitation 
and basic first aid. 

* Megan Wynne-Jones, M.D., Re¬ 
search Assistant, Lyndhurst Lodge 
Hospital. 

Bibliography 

1. Harrison, T. R., Principles of 
Internal Medicine, McGraw-Hill 
Book Co., New York. 

2. W. O. Geisler, M.D., M. Wynne- 
Jones, M.D., and A. T. Jousse, 
M.D., “Early Management of the 
Patient ivith Trauma to the 
Spinal Cord”, Medical Services 
Journal Canada, Volume XXII, 
No. 7, pages 512-522, July- 
August, 1966, Veterans Affairs 
Building, Ottawa, Canada. 

3. Wm. O. Geisler and A. T. 
Jousse, “Management of the 
Spinal Injured Patient”, Modern 
Medicine of Canada, December, 
1968. 

4. A. T. Jousse, M.D., “The Man¬ 
agement of Paraplegia’’, Mani¬ 
toba Medical Review, Vol. 43, 
No. 7, August-September 1963, 
Pp. 383 to 391. 

5. Dr. Zudwig Guttman, “Neuro¬ 
logical Injuries Sustained 
Through Diving’’, British Asso¬ 
ciation of Sport and Medicine 
Bulletin, Vol. 1, No. 2, 1964

Our Indebtedness 
to Our Indian Friends 

by Mary S. Edgar 
Honorary Chairman, 

Canadian Camping Association 

A talk given in the Glen Bernard Camp chapel, 
Sunday, August fifteenth, 197b os part of the 
Fiftieth Anniversary ceremonies . 


Miss Mary Edgar 



The news that Glen Bernard was 
having a new totem pole carved for 
this fiftieth anniversary year, gave 
me great satisfaction. The old totem 
pole which stands at the entrance 
to the Glen was carved by campers 
long ago, but Time and the wood¬ 
peckers have done serious damage 
to it, probably beyond Repair. 

The new totem pole now taking 
shape at Camp under the skilled 
craftsmanship of Mr. Tom Bowie of 
Ontario College of Art will be 
much taller and more impressive. It 
will proclaim for many years Glen 
Bernard’s continuing interest in the 
Indians. 

Every camper who has been here 
knows that in this place there has 
always been a deep respect for the 
traditions, the symbols and the leg¬ 
ends of the Indians. Every camper 
has been made a member of a tribe. 
Practically every Saturday evening 
for fifty summers the tribes have 
gathered in the Council Ring for a 
ceremony which is both entertain¬ 
ing and inspiring. 

Having often been asked, “How 
did you get the idea of the Indian 
theme?” That could be a long story, 
but briefly it is — 

When I was ten years old the 
famous Pauline Johnson “the Mo¬ 
hawk Princess” gave a program of 
her dramatic poems in Sundridge 
and was a guest in our home. I was 
fascinated, and wished I were re¬ 
lated to her. The following summer 
of 1900 on a fishing trip with my 
father on Lake Nipissing, our 
launch stopped in a storm. At the 
mercy of wind and waves we were 
rescued by two Indian friends of my 


father from the Dokis Reserve. In 
two canoes they managed to get the 
four of us safely to Sturgeon Falls. 
We felt that we owed our lives to 
them. We had a debt to pay. 

During my Y.W.C.A. training 
course in New York 1914-15, where 
I specialized in Club and Camp 
work, I met several outstanding 
Camp leaders. Miss Ruby M. 
Jolliffe, who became a life-long 
friend, was Superintendent of State 
Camps for New York and New 
Jersey. At her Bear Mountain cabin 
I met “Princess Ti-ata” from a 
southern tribe. She was a superb 
story-teller and “Jolly” often en¬ 
gaged her for Council Ring pro¬ 
grams. They gave me a great deal 
of information on Indian traditions 
and customs. 

When I was director of Camp 
Oolahwan in the Laurentians, (the 
Montreal Y.W.C.A. camp), it was 
difficult to have a council ring cere¬ 
mony, for our campers changed 
practically every week. In July 1921 
when I returned with my parents 
from a trip around the world, I was 
eager to get to work on my dream 
— “a camp of my own”. On the first 
trip to my new property on Lake 
Bernard I discovered the Glen, a 
perfect amphitheatre for a Council 
ring. It seemed quite natural then 
to name the new camp Glen 
Bernard. 

We need often to remind our¬ 
selves that this country which we 
proudly call “This land of Ours”, 
once belonged to the Indians. The 
stone-mason who built the stone 
wall and patio of High Rock found 
an Indian arrow-head near there. 


There is therefore no doubt that 
the first trails of these forests were 
made by the moccasined feet of the 
Algonquins or the Ojibways. It was 
the smoke from their camp-fires 
which first ascended to the sky, and 
it was their bark canoes that were 
paddled in the sunlight or the 
moonlight across the lake. 

We have been privileged over the 
years to have three outstanding 
Indians as guests at Glen Bernard. 

The first one was Dawendine, the 
daughter of a Mohawk chief from 
the Six Nations’ Reserve. In 1934 
when I read a newspaper item 
about a talk she had given in Brant¬ 
ford, I promptly wrote and invited 
her to be a guest at our Camp 
Banquet at the Granite Club. She 
came, and we were so thrilled with 
her stories, that we persuaded her 
to visit Camp, where she made such 
a happy contribution that we 
named a cabin after her. 

Again the following summer she 
returned but she did not specify 
when she would arrive. Early one 
morning I was awakened by some¬ 
one tapping on my door. On open¬ 
ing it, I found Dawendine standing 
there, with a suitcase in one hand 
and a paddle in the other. 

“Why how did you get here?” I 
exclaimed. 

Her lovely brown eyes twinkled 
as she said, “I walked! It was a 
beautiful morning. I had the world 
to myself.” 

“But that train came in about 
five o’clock, and it is four and a 
half miles from the station. Who 
carried the suitcase and the pad¬ 
dle?” I asked. 


13 


“I did!” she said merrily. “My 
name means ‘Dawn’ in Mohawk, or 
“that time before the birds begin 
to sing.” 

Then she placed in my hands the 
beautiful paddle saying, “This is a 
gift to you from my father. He 
chose the young maple tree, cut it 
down himself and shaped the pad¬ 
dle. I decorated it with the draw¬ 
ings. Each one is the totem of one 
of our Six tribes. The wolf is the 
totem or emblem of our tribe, the 
Mohawks.” 

That paddle was treasured great¬ 
ly by me and was used on every 
trip I made by canoe from that day 
on. I took it away with me when I 
retired, but when Dawendine re¬ 
turned to Camp in 1969 I gave it 
back to her, in memory of her 
father. 

Dawendine delighted us with her 
stories which she generously shared 
in Council ring, in chapel, or to 
small and large groups around our 
fires. Often they were dramatic but 
the one I would like to tell you 
was a simple story from her own 
childhood which the younger 
campers particularly enjoyed. 

“When I was a small child,” she 
said, “I made friends with a mouse. 
My wee pal became so tame she 
would come to me every day and 
eat crumbs out of my hand. One 
day I thought, ‘My mouse is going 
to become a Mother-Mouse,’ and 1 
watched for her with more interest. 
But, for several days she did not 
return and I was worried. Finally 
however, I saw my mouse limping 
towards me, struggling along, trying 
to carry one of her fragile babies. 
Depositing it beside me she disap¬ 
peared. Slowly however she made 
two more difficult trips, each time 
returning with a very tiny mouse. 
Then I sadly realized that the 
mother-mouse knew she was going 
to die and she was placing her little 
ones in my care. I was deeply 
touched that she trusted me to care 
for them. I never saw her again but 
I respected her faith in me and 
every day the little orphans were 
fed regularly with milk from an 
eyedropper. Under my care the 
three of them thrived and I felt a 
bit sad when they were strong 
enough to scamper away and look 
after themselves.” 

This story illustrates Dawen- 
dine’s deep reverence for all living 


creatures. This reverence for life 
was part of the Indian’s religion. 
Gitchee Manitou the Great-Spirit 
was in all things he had created. 

Our next important Indian guest 
was Chief Mudjeekwis of the Ojib- 
ways from the Rice Lake reserva¬ 
tion. 

His story is told in verse in 
“Woodfire and Candlelight” but 
briefly it is this: 

We were all gathered in the Glen 
awaiting his arrival. “At last he 
came, true Indian chief, With slow 
and stately tread, a crown of eagle 
feathers Upon his noble head. Fire 
tenders added fuel, Again the 
flames rose high. The birches stood 
out slim and white Against the 
dark night sky.” Then Mudjeekwis 
told this legend. 

“Long ago a Chief of the Ojib- 
ways had a daughter whom he 
dearly loved, but she was often 
very sad. ‘Why are you so sad,* he 
asked, ‘when I want you to be 
happy?’ She answered, ‘I will be 
happy if you give me a camp-site of 
my own by the lake, where every 
day I can have with me the children 
of the tribe.’ 

‘Why would you take them from 
their wigwams?’ 

‘Because,’ she said, ‘no one has 
time to teach them anything. The 
Braves have their hunting and fish¬ 
ing, the women have their cooking. 
The children have nothing to do 
and they quarrel a lot.’ 

‘What would you teach them?’ he 
asked. 

I would teach them all I know. 
How to use the bow and arrows, 
how to paddle, how to make things 
from reeds, barks and leather. But 
most of all I would tell them stories 
of our race, legends old and new.’ 

So the Chief gave to his daughter 
the camp-site she desired. Not only 
was she happy but day after day 
she kept the children busy and 
happy.” 

After Chief Mudjeekwis had fin¬ 
ished this story, he turned to me 
and said, “I would now ask you to 
stand down in front of me.” To the 
surprise of us all he said: “I honor 
now your chief, Her name in camp 
shall be Ogimagua, Children’s 
friend, in happy memory.” It was 
thus that I acquired the Indian 
name of Ogimagua. 

My successor, Barbara Gilchrist 
who has presided over the Council 


Ring for sixteen summers was given 
her Indian name by Dawendine. It 
is “Yeh-jenh-hi-yos-tah” (sounding 
Ye-jen-e-yos-ta) meaning “One who 
keeps the fire burning”. That name 
is appropriate for both the Gil¬ 
christs. Not only have they kept the 
Council Ring fire burning, but also 
the fires of friendship and camp 
spirit. 

The next exceptional guest who 
visited us was ‘Nanaki” of the 
Blackfeet Indians, a great tribe of 
the western plains. Knowing no in¬ 
ternational boundaries, they ex¬ 
tended through Wyoming, Alberta 
and into the foothills of the 
Rockies. 

It was by lucky chance that we 
happened to get Nanaki for Coun¬ 
cil Ring. She was one of a small 
group of Indians from across Can¬ 
ada who was chosen to represent 
our country at the coronation of 
Queen Elizabeth. 

On the ship coming back from 
England, Helen Stewart, a former 
camper-counselor, made her ac- 
quaintenance, and interested her in 
our Council Ring ceremony. Finally 
Helen said, “would you stop over 
and visit Glen Bernard before you 
return to your western reserve? I’d 
go up with you.” When Helen 
phoned, I said we’d be greatly 
honoured to have her, and a few 
days later they arrived. 

It was a thrill of surprise for us 
when Nanaki descended the steps 
to the Council Ring wearing her 
elaborately beaded white doe skin 
costume and head band — the outfit 
made specially for her appearance 
at the coronation. 

But it was not only her appear¬ 
ance which made a deep and lasting 
impression. It was her message. She 
said, in part, “You have heard how 
fortunate I have been in being one 
of the few chosen to represent my 
people at the coronation of our 
Queen. Because of the exceptional 
blessings and opportunities I have 
enjoyed, I have a debt to pay. I in¬ 
tend to go back to my people and 
share all I have with them. You too, 
have been very generously endowed 
with good gifts — health, and edu¬ 
cation. You too have a debt to pay. 
There are many with so much less 
than you. “To whom much is given, 
from her much is expected.” Pay 
what you owe to Life.” 

Continued on Page 20

Age Group Characteristics in Camp 

by Brian Blackstock 
Director, Camp Mazinaw 


The following article was written 
to assist Camp Leaders in their staff 
training programs so that some 
common characteristics of boys at 
various age levels can be noted. 
Most of the information in the ar¬ 
ticle comes from a recent study 
done at Camp Mazinaw by the 
author. This study was made pos¬ 
sible by the financial assistance of 
The Neathern Trust and presented 
at an earlier date to The Society of 
Camp Directors. 

There seem to be two main rea¬ 
sons why children enjoy living in a 
natural environment: 

1. It is not a world made for 
adults in which children also 
live. 

2. The natural environment is 
the same for children as it is 
for adults and its constant state 
of change is more obvious. 

Here is a world they are free to 
explore — to live in an environment 
where children and adults must 
have similar values — a world where 
they will discern that the “GAP” 
in our society is not one of 
“GENERATION” but one of 
“VALUES”. 

Age Group Characteristics 
in Camp 

8-9 years 

— very energetic, short attention 
spans 

— need to learn to be imaginative 
in new directions 

— very dependent on counsellor/ 
instructor for direction and sup¬ 
port 

— short periods of independence 
are useful 

— enjoy games of pretend 

— very conscious of their limited 
skills 

— take pride in each skill step for¬ 
ward 

— enjoy special projects which in¬ 


volve only their group 

— short trips to new places are ap¬ 
pealing 

— ability of counsellor to be imag¬ 
inative is important 

— fearful of the environment until 
they get used to it 

— like competition if they feel they 
have some chance of success 

— acceptance by cabinmates is es¬ 
sential 

— tend to be more self-centred than 
older campers 

— often spirits go up and down 
with the weather, fear of the 
dark and storms is not yet over¬ 
come 

9-11 years 

— continue to enjoy much activity, 
particularly bush games 

— want to develop skills so they can 
assure a degree of some inde¬ 
pendence 

— want some specific counsellor 
leadership 

— counsellors should do less overt 
leading 

— often attempt too much too soon 
— counsellors can be very helpful 
in controlling this 

— becoming interested in specifics 
in the environment 

— being a member of a group re¬ 
quires campers to adapt to the 
group and to the environment — 
this is sometimes hard 

— like to prove and improve their 
physical skills 

— some appreciation is developing 
for crafts 

— enjoy searching out interesting 
adults to talk with 

— group is a stronger motivator 
than standardized tests 

— being alone is of some interest 
but not of great importance 

— long periods of poor weather dis¬ 
courages them 

— activities such as cooking, canoe¬ 
ing, passing tests should have an 
obvious purpose, ie — to live 


more comfortably in the bush 

— especially enjoy music 

11- 12 years 

— are becoming more thoughtful as 
physical skills increase 

— like trips of limited length (3-4 
days) 

— have difficulty in accepting fail¬ 
ure 

— still have some fear of the bush 

— enjoy exploring and games which 
will make them more familiar 
with the bush 

— are keen to improve skills, try to 
emulate older campers 

— acceptance of natural phenom¬ 
ena, such as storms, is better 

— like group projects but also ap¬ 
preciate times when they can be 
alone knowing some staff person 
is available 

— confidence can come from the 
friendship of one or two peers — 
acceptance by the large group is 
no longer essential 

— standardized tests are stronger 
motivations than when younger 

— developing pleasure, and skill in 
cooking on trips 

— beginning to be concerned about 
ability to make themselves com¬ 
fortable in the bush for longer 
periods of time 

— still enjoy a variety of activities 
—attention span increasing 

— value being accepted as an im¬ 
portant member of “the group” 

— counsellors role is increasingly 
supportive rather than directive 

12- 13 years 

— want new challenges to prove 
acquired skills 

— like the idea of the challenge of 
trips where the unexpected may 
occur 

— meet weather changes better, 
more as a challenge to be over¬ 
come 

— standardized tests are good moti¬ 
vators as they seem to develop the 


15 


Ccimp Mazinaw 



confidence they want 

— crafts continue to arouse increas¬ 
ing interest 

— need more time to be alone 

— appreciate quiet time with cabin- 
mates 

— like to explore 

— sailing is becoming of greater 
interest 

— interested in survival, eg. finding 
natural foods 

— enjoy meeting new people 

— food preparation is of greater 
interest 

— five or six day trips are popular 
because of adventure factor 

— the animals of the bush arouse 
much interest 

— fishing is of limited interest 

— need to be allowed more inde¬ 
pendence by adults but value 
recognition for their achieve¬ 
ments 

— counsellor's role has now become 
one of die “able older brother” 
in whom campers have confidence 

13-14 years 

— can take long periods of involve¬ 
ment if their elders do not inter¬ 
fere too often — comment after 
activity is best 

— becoming more aware of the 


subtleties of nature and man's 
interdependence 

— like to prove acquired skills on 
challenging trips 

— are aware of the need for co¬ 
operation, particularly on trips 

— appreciate privacy, value a few 
close friends 

— counsellors who support their in¬ 
terests are appreciated 

— single sports becoming more at¬ 
tractive 

— sharing ideas/discussions with 
and without counsellors are im¬ 
portant 

— sensitive to criticism 

— acceptance by others is important 

— personal goals are being formed 
and strived for 

15-16 years 

— counsellors should be very ob¬ 
servant but in the background 

— “silent lessons” — by example are 
most effective 

— individual skills continue to in¬ 
crease in importance 

— have more self-discipline than 
younger campers 

— more aware of the value of work¬ 
ing together 

— like reflective type music occa¬ 
sionally 


— passing along their skills and 
knowledge to those less exper¬ 
ienced is important 

— becoming concerned with the 
quality of the environment 

— enjoy using the wilderness as a 
food source 

— need periods of free time and 
opportunities to be “lazy” and 
alone 

— like trying challenging recipes on 
trips 

— increasing interest in subtle 
things like sunsets, the beauty of 
the bush 

— are good organizers of trips, need 
little direction 

— times to be alone and think are 
important 

— serious discussions with peers are 
of value 

“It’s a good thing when a person 
is different from your image of him. 
It shows he isn’t a type. If he were, 
it would be the end of him as a 
man. But if you can’t place him in 
a category, it means that at least 
part of him is what a human being 
ought to be. He is free from him¬ 
self, he has a grain of immortality.” 

Boris Pasternak in 
“Dr. Zhivago”

WHAT’S WITH YOUR STORAGE 


Do you save 


Can your supplies and equip¬ 
ment take it as temperatures drop 
far, far below zero? Must you hire a 
truck to bring to the city all perish¬ 
ables, breakables and leak-ables? Or 
perhaps you are one of those luckies 
with year-round heated buildings 
in which everything can be left in 
readiness for the Spring opening. 
For those who work on a half-camp- 
half-city basis, Canadian Camping 
has gathered this material for the 
benefit of new camp directors in 
particular, but for the further edi¬ 
fication of those who have been in 
the business for some years. There 
may be some hints from which we 
can all profit and enjoy peace of 
mind: 

PIANO — a mildly warm room 
with an even temperature (this is 
important) makes for ideal storing. 
If this is not available, there’s no 
alternative but to leave the piano 
in place at camp to face the winter 
completely uncovered (also impor¬ 
tant) with the keyboard exposed. 
DO NOT cover with blankets or 
tarp. This holds in dampness to 
rust strings and damage felts. A cup 
of powdered camphor scattered in¬ 
side the instrument will discourage 
mice. 

SMALL MUSICAL INSTRU¬ 
MENTS — should be taken to the 
city if heated accommodation is not 
available. 

MEDICAL SUPPLIES - all medi¬ 
cations, drugs, pills, especially 
liquids, should be returned to the 
city, and all supplies replenished 
for the following summer. Pills and 
drugs deteriorate in temperature 
changes. ASA and other tablets 


money as you care for your equipment during 
/ the winter months? 

by Eanswythe Flynn 


crumble. Adhesive perishes. Ab¬ 
sorbent cotton and gauze are sheer 
heaven for mice condominiums. 
FLASHLIGHTS - the cases re¬ 
main at camp, but for heavens’ sake 
remove batteries. Check bulbs in 
the spring. 

HOT WATER BOTTLES - may 
be left, hanging upside down with 
the stoppers removed. By the way, 
do you tie, with a length of cord, 
each stopper to the top of each 
bottle? Saves frantic searching at 
the moment when they have just 
been filled. 

MATTRESSES - should be left on 
the beds, sprinkled generously with 
naphtha flakes and cedar fronds or 
powdered camphor. As heat caus¬ 
ing combustion forms in the centre 
of a stack of piled mattresses, our 
Fire Department advisers tell us 
NEVER to stack them for storage, 
summer or winter. 

PAINTS — must be kept in a warm 
room. If there isn’t one at camp 
take them back to the city; and this 
includes varnish, Solignum, shellac, 
and tubes of artists’s paints from 
the craft shop. 

WAX AND OILS -- floor wax, lin¬ 
seed oil, machine oils, Hippo Oil 
and other oils for cleaning may re¬ 
main at camp. Low temperatures 
do not affect them for good use in 
the summer. 

COAL OIL OR STOVE OIL - 
may be left at camp in a safe stor¬ 
age space approved by the Fire 
Marshal. 

GASOLINE — may be left at camp, 
stored in a safe place approved by 
the Fire Marshal. This must be a 
place removed from other stored 


items. 

PROPANE — turn off taps at out¬ 
door tanks which can be left as they 
are during the winter. 

FIRE EXTINGUISHERS—should 
be thoroughly checked and referred 
to the Fire Marshal for storage and 
re-charging. 

VINEGARS — will survive provid¬ 
ing the bottles are only two-thirds 
to three-quarters full. 

OTHER LIQUIDS - all should be 
removed, including juices, soft 
drinks, syrups, flavourings, concen¬ 
trates. 

CANNED GOODS - always store 
in the city if there is no warm room 
year-round at camp. Never use after 
freezing. As a rule, tinned Lood 
bursts in freezing. 

DRV STAPLES - flour, sugar, 
powdered milk, dry cereals, potato 
flakes, jelly and pudding powders 
(not powdered egg) dehydrated 
vegetables, soups and trip meals 
may be left, stored TIGHTLY in 
sealed pails or the heavy plastic 
garbage pails used in summer for 
storing staples. 

RUGS — remove them from the 
floor. Mice tear them apart. 
Threads and tufts form the perfect 
interior decor for nests and new 
mice babies. 

BLANKETS — a cupboard lined 
with metal or wire window screen¬ 
ing, or trunks with secure fastenings 
are the only places to keep blankets, 
pillows, linens, washable rugs and 
mats. A large cupboard of this type 
is a good investment for storage 
without benefit of mice and squir¬ 
rels.

Enjoyment of Mutual Aid Holidays 

by Mme Nicol, Mme Grenier, M. Boisueit, 

Guy Duchesne, Lucille Verreault 
translated by Jean Darrach 


From the 26th of June to the 10th 
of July, 12 families of the St. Jean 
Baptiste quarter of Montreal spent 
a holiday at Lac des Plages. Most of 
these families had not had a proper 
vacation for many years. Some had 
given up the idea that they would 
ever be able to leave the city for a 
holiday. Yet, here they were taking 
part in the first family camp held 
for people of this part of the city. 

THE BEGINNING 

Three people who worked in St. 
Jean Baptiste and were responsible 
for initiating the camp, had had 
family camp experience in other 
places and believed it was a real 
possibility for these St. Jean Bap¬ 
tiste families. 

Once financing was assured 
through the Department of Family 
and Social Welfare and the Riche¬ 
lieu Club, it was proposed at a 
meeting of the twelve families that 
they should organize and carry out 
a plan for the two-week camping 
holiday. All agreed to attend the 
planning meetings and to be re¬ 
sponsible for the food bills for their 
own families at camp. They took 
up the challenge of working to¬ 
gether to realize a dream they 
would have thought impossible just 
a few months earlier. 

From the first meeting the success 
of the project was entirely in the 
hands of the families themselves 
and everyone set to work to plan a 
camp that would satisfy all the par¬ 
ticipants. 

From April until June the fam¬ 
ilies held regular planning meet¬ 
ings. Decisions about transporta¬ 
tion, purchase of games equipment, 
camp activities, monitoring duties, 
purchase of food, and so on, v/ere 
taken after all opinions were heard. 
Representatives were chosen and 
tasks assigned. The meetings al¬ 


lowed the parents to become well 
acquainted and establish a “group” 
feeling that stood them in good 
stead during the two weeks at Lac 
des Plages. 

THE DREAM COME TRUE 

At the campsite each family had 
its own cabin and did its own cook¬ 
ing. From time to time all the fam¬ 
ilies had a meal together in connec¬ 
tion with some community activity: 
church service, a ball game, camp¬ 
fire, a dance or sing-song. 

During the afternoon, leaders 
trained as a project of Perspective- 
Jeunesse, conducted activities for 
the children: swimming, ball games, 
art and crafts. At the same time the 
parents had their own activities: 
horseshoes, swimming, baseball, 
boating, badminton. 

Other activities that should be 
mentioned: a raspberry picking ex¬ 
pedition, an overnight camp for the 
teenagers, a social evening at the 
local hotel for the parents and a 
fishing trip. 

All these activities were organ¬ 
ized by the group. Those who had 
the initial ideas passed them on to 
the others and, if they were ac¬ 
cepted, the organization was carried 
out by the members of the group. 
On the other hand, no one was 
obliged to take part in any activity. 
Everyone iclt free to take part or 
not as the spirit moved. There was 
a good deal of inter-visiting among 
the cottages and people from town 
came to visit also. 

Mutual support among the fam¬ 
ilies was characteristic of the camp. 
Spontaneously all came to the aid 
of those who got into difficulties. 
One of the mothers was kept busy 
helping families with sick children. 
The women did the laundry for 
those who were unable. Those who 
had cars looked after the transpor¬ 
tation of the others. 


THE FOLLOW-UP 

When they returned to town, 
most of the families wanted to keep 
in touch. Evenings were organized 
to view films and slides taken at 
camp. Then other activities — a 
knitting group, dances, baptism 
parties. Many families have gone on 
visiting and helping each other. 

Some regular meetings have also 
been arranged to prepare for next 
year’s camp. Many new projects 
have been proposed and all have 
aired their opinions. The new 
meetings are keeping the members 
in charge of planning the vacation 
and it is clear that the group will 
enlarge because five new families 
have already joined. 

A GREAT EXPERIENCE 

Two weeks in which each person 
is accepted for what he is, his help 
is accepted by others, he never feels 
left out because he has no money, 
or is handicapped, or separated or 
because his children are unruly. 
Each is permitted to ofler his tal¬ 
ents, to establish bonds and to 
make friends. 

Good country air and freedom 
from daily chores, the help of the 
others: these arc the factors that 
give the parents a chance to think 
and recover their strength. Family 
relationships are also revived and 
improved by the experience. 

To make contact with others, to 
take part and resolve difficulties, to 
have many occasions for involve¬ 
ment, to have self-confidence, to 
help others, are finally to help one’s 
self to solve personal problems. By 
means of such an experience people 
discover how much they can accom¬ 
plish by working together. 

Learning to know oneself and 
how to live together co-operatively 
arc sometimes difficult but the re¬ 
wards are tremendous. 

(“RELATIONS” - Nov. 1971)

Plaisirs de l’entraide 

et des vacances 


— l’experience du camp familial 
Saint-Jean-Baptiste recon tee par un 
groupe de citoyens du quartier — 
en collaboration: Mine Nicol, Mine 
Grenier, M. Boisvert, Guy Du¬ 
chesne, Lucille Verreault. 

Du 26 juin au 10 juillet, douze 
families du quartier Saint-Jean- 
Baptiste, de Montreal, se retrouvent 
en vacances au Lac-des-Plages. La 
plupart de ces families n'ont pas 
beneficie de vacances depuis plu- 
sieurs annees et certaines ont meme 
cesse de croire qu’il leur serait un 
jour possible de jouir de vacances a 
Pexterieur de la ville. Maintenant, 
elles participent a une experience 
de camp familial ten tee pour la 
premiere fois dans ce secteur de la 
ville. 

On Commence 

Cette initiative a cte suscitee par 
trois personnes travaillant dans ce 
quartier. Connaissant les expe¬ 
riences realisees a divers autres en- 
droits, elles ont cm a la possibility 
d un camp familial dans Saint-Jean- 
Baptiste. 

Une fois le financement assure 
(Ministere des Affaires sociales, 
Club Richelieu), douze families 
sont regroupees et on leur propose 
d'organiser et de realiser ensemble 
un camp de deux semaines dont 
elles beneficieraient. Le projet exige 
de chacune qu'elle participe aux 
reunions de preparation et qu’elle 
assure le paiement de sa nourriture 
au moment du camp. Toutes ac- 
ceptent de relever le defi et de se 
mettre ensemble pour realiser ce 
reve qu’elles croyaient impossible a 
peine quelqucs mois auparavant. 
Des cet instant, la reussite du pro¬ 
jet est entre les mains des families 
et cliacun se sert de son imagina¬ 
tion pour que le camp satisfasse 
tous les participants. 


D’avril a juin, les families se 
fixent des reunions regulieres pour 
cette preparation. Les decisions 
pour Forganisation (transport, ac¬ 
tivites, achat dequipement de jeux, 
moniteurs, achat de la nourriture, 
etc.) se prennent en respectant les 
opinions de chacun. Des represen- 
tants du groupe sont elus et deja 
certaines laches sont reparties. Ces 
rencontres permettent aux parents 
de se connaitre et de former un 
groupe qui se retrouvera avec plai- 
sir pendant deux semaines au Lac- 
des-Plages. 

On realise 

Au Lac-des-Plages, chacun pos¬ 
sible son chalet et fait sa nourriture. 
De temps en temps, des repas re- 
groupent toutes les families; ces 
repas sont precedes ou suivis d’ac- 
tivites communautaires (messe, jcu 
de ballon, feux de camp, danses, 
chansons « a repondre », etc.). 

L’apres-midi, des moniteurs pro¬ 
tes par un projet de Perspectives- 
Jeunesse s’occupent des enfants: 
jeux de ballon, plage, arts plas- 
tiques, etc. Pendant ce temps, les 
parents se rejoignent pour aller a 
la plage ou pour certaines activites: 
jeux de fer, de sacs de sable, pro¬ 
menade en cludoupe, baseball, bad¬ 
minton. 

Parmi les autres activites, on peut 
mentionner: une cueillette de 

fraises, une nuit de camping pour 
les adolescents, une soiree a l’hotel 
pour les parents, la peche . . . 

Toutes ces activites s’organisent 
spontanement. Ceux qui ont des 
idees les suggerent aux autres et, si 
elles sont acceptees, les activites 
s’organisent avec la collaboration 
de tout le monde. Par ailleurs, au- 
cune de ces activites n’est obliga- 
toire, chacun se sent libre cl’y par- 
ticiper s’il en a envie. II arrive sou- 


vent egalement que les families se 
visitent dans leurs chalets respectils 
ou que des gens de Pexterieur vien- 
nent se joindre au groupe. 

L’entraide entre les families est 
l un des traits marquants de ce 
camp. Spontanement, on vient en 
aide a ceux qui ont des difficultes: 
une mere se prcoccupe d’aider les 
autres quand leurs enfants sont 
malades, des femmes font le lavage 
pour ceux qui ne pen vent le faire, 
ceux qui posscdent des autos trans¬ 
portent les families cloignees . . . 
Plusieurs personnes du quartier ou 
de Pexterieur ont egalement aide le 
groupe pour le transport des fa¬ 
milies au Lac-des-Plages, ou encore 
par des dons. 

On continue 

De retour a la ville, la plupart 
des families ont le gout de garder 
contact avec les autres. Des soirees 
rccreatives s’organisent pour revoir 
les films ou diapositives du camp. 
On sc retrouve egalement dans 
d’alitres activites du milieu (soirees 
de danse, groupe tricot, marraines 
. . .). Plusieurs families continuent 
a se visiter et a se rendre service. 

Des rencontres plus formclles 
sont egalement realisees pour pre¬ 
parer Pan prochain. Plusieurs pro¬ 
jets sont proposes et chacun ex¬ 
prime son opinion sur ce qu’il de¬ 
sire. Ces rencontres vont permettre 
au groupe de continuer a prendre 
en charge la realisation de ses va¬ 
cances. On peut prevoir que le 
groupe va s’agrandir puisque deja 
cinq families s’y sont jointes. 

Une experience formidable: 
pourquoi? 

Deux semaines ou chacun est 
accepte comme il est, ou il apporte 
sa collaboration aux autres, ou il ne

Continued from Page 14 

It will be of interest to you that 
Nanaki’s English name is Norah 
Gladstone. Her father was the late 
Senator Gladstone, the only Indian 
who has ever been chosen to sit in 
the Senate of our country. He re¬ 
tired last spring. 

Have we not been fortunate in¬ 
deed in the three who have repre¬ 
sented the Indian race! How much 
they have shared with us. 

The old campers as a fiftieth year 
project raised a fund to bring In¬ 
dian girls to Camp this summer, 
but we found it takes time to work 
out worth- while arrangements. 
However, by next year, the second 
half-century, we will have had suffi¬ 
cient time to scout and find girls for 
whom the experience of Camp life 
at Glen Bernard will be of great 
value. In any case, we are counting 
on having Dawendine with us as 
our special guest for the Granite 
Club reunion in September. 

Life Magazine had a special edi¬ 
tion in July, featuring the story of 
the Indian on this continent. It is a 
sad story. It is a story to make one 
blush with shame. They have not 
had a fair deal. Many in our land 
are among the poorest of the poor. 

Governments, churches and many 
organizations are becoming increas¬ 
ingly aware of the sad plight of 
many of our Indian citizens. In 
every part of our land there is a 
new concern which should result in 
a better life for them. 

Yet we hope the Indians will 
treasure their old legends, customs 
and traditions and that the white 
race will learn to appreciate those 
things that are unique and precious 
in their culture. 

Quoting from a poem by our 
friend Dawendine, (a tribute to her 
father Chief Sahrenhowane of the 
Mohawks) 

“He wove a spell by stories 

Of old Iroquian days, 

Of turtle shell and wampum 
beads; 

The age-old League of Peace 

Was born anew under his magic 
tongue/* 

If we aspire to be a Christian 
country, let us remember and fol¬ 
low the Golden Rule given us by 
Jesus, “Do unto others as you would 
they should do unto you/* Let us 
try by friendship and service to pay 
a debt which is long over-due. 



George Sharpe 
by Eanswythe Flynn 
Surely no one was quite so well 
known to most of us in the Cana¬ 
dian Camping Association as was 
George Sharpe, “Mr. Gibbons 
Foods". His passing last June came 
as a shock to us in the Fall, though 
we knew that he had been under 
his doctor’s care for some time. At 
the Ontario, Quebec and Maritimes 
Camping Conferences and in Wes¬ 
tern Canada, his warm personality 
and good humour won many 
friends who benefitted as well from 
his personal interest, his timely 
advice and sound suggestions. 
George became president of the 
firm on the death of his father-in- 
law who founded the company. It 
was due to Mr. Sharpe’s energy and 
business accumen that Gibbon’s 
Foods continued to expand. To 
Mrs. Sharpe and their daughter and 
to the members of his staff Cana¬ 
dian Camping extends sympathy in 
the loss of a good friend. 



TANYA KRISMAN 
by John Latimer 

The sad neius of the tragic death 
in a motor accident of Tanya Kris- 
man on April 28 was indeed a deep 
shock to her many friends in camp¬ 
ing across this Country. 

Tanya has contributed much to 
the camping scene in Canada, and 
as a Vice-President of the Canadian 
Camping Association — Association 
des Camps du Canada — we all 
knew that she gave freely and 
openly of her time and tremendous 
talent. 

This summer one of Tanya's 
dreams was to become a reality. 
For some time, as an active worker 
with the Y.W.C.A. in Vancouver, 
Tanya had envisioned a year-round 
Outdoor Centre on Salt Spri?igs Is- 
land. In her capacity as Director 
of this new Camp, YaWaCa, she 
would have continued to pursue 
her faith and beliefs in young peo¬ 
ple by developing them through in¬ 
volvement and above all trust. 

Sadly, Tanya leaves behind her 
husband and tioo young daughters. 
But she also leaves her dreams with 
us. It is now up to us to perpetuate 
these dreams to ensure that YaWa¬ 
Ca becomes a truly living memorial 
to a very warm, sincere, fine hu¬ 
man being.

James C. Moore 

by Eanswythe Flynn 

The death of James C. Moore, 
on Saturday, July 10, 1971, brought 
to a close a life of dedication and 
service to the Boy Scouts of Canada 
and to Canadian Camping. J.C., as 
he was affectionately known by all 
who came in contact with him, had 
been ill for the previous three years, 
but continued to participate active¬ 
ly in Camping and, in particular, 
with the Halibut ton Scout Reserve. 
J.C. had been involved with the 
Haliburton Scout Reserve from its 
founding in 1947 with a few ex¬ 
perimental Camps being held to 
1970 when there were approximate¬ 
ly 350 Campers per week in atten¬ 
dance. 

“J.C.” was active for many years 
with the Ontario Camping Associa¬ 
tion as a representative of the Boy 
Scouts of Canada, Greater Toronto 
Region, and a member of the 
Board. 

From the eulogy given by Ian E. 
Jones, Camp Staff Member of the 
Haliburton Scout Reserve, lie ex¬ 
pressed the thoughts of all who 
knew Jim Moore: 

“. .. the nature of J.C.’s character 
made his personality vital and dy¬ 
namic and each one of us have 
unique and personal memories of 
times we shared with him. Some 
will always think of Jim as a de¬ 
voted husband and understanding 
father. Some will remember him as 
a trusted companion and friend. 
Others will think of him as an 
adventurous and exciting leader. 
And many young people who never 
knew his name will remember J.C. 
as the man in that bright uniform 
who was always there with an un¬ 
derstanding look and a kind word 
when things went wrong. 

“To confine memories of J.C. to 
words of description and stories of 
old times is to attempt the impos¬ 
sible. Knowing him was a feeling: 
a feeling as inspiring as hope and 
as unmistakable as love. It is a 
feeling which may be different for 
everyone who knew him — but it is 
a feeling that will be part of us all 
forever.”

Continued from Page 17 
SADDLES — and all leather goods 
should be well saddle-soaped be¬ 
fore hanging. Proppert’s and God¬ 
dard’s Saddle Soaps are best. Never 
use floor wax or liquid furniture 
wax. 

OFFICE SUPPLIES - If you leave 
envelopes for the winter, packaged 
or not, they will automatically seal, 
beyond all hope of using. Letter¬ 
head and copy papers can stay if 
they are flat and dry with a weight 
or large book covering the 8 X 10 
area. Marking pens, felt pens 
Scripto or Bik pens deteriorate. 
Bottled inks and scotch tape sur¬ 
vive. Stamp pads need only re¬ 
inking for the new season. Craft 
paper, newsprint, bristol board and 
construction paper must be stored 
flat on the floor or table top, 
weighted down so that corners 
cannot curl, in a mouse-proof room. 
If doors are open to such nibblers, 
take these papers to the city. 
PAINT BRUSHES - should al¬ 
ways be thoroughly cleaned after 
each use during the spring and 
summer. There are excellent . . . 
almost magic . . . cleaners on the 
market now that will soften even 
moderately hard bristles; but there 
is no hope once they have hardened 
over the winter months, frozen and 
melted. A considerable fortune can 
be saved by taking care of them 
after use, soaking in turpentine or 
Dick-a-Doo, rinsing in warm deter¬ 
gent suds, then clear water. Hang 
them by a string to dry in the sun¬ 
shine. Failing that system, try Tri¬ 
sodium Phosphate or hot vinegar, 
rinse in suds, then clear water and 
hang outside to dry. 

RAGS that have been used for 
paint, brush cleaning or oils must 
be removed to the local dump. 
Don’t put them in the camp incin¬ 
erator. Oily rags form one of the 
greatest fire hazards, and can create 
an uncontrolled quick blaze in the 
incinerator. 

WATER SYSTEM - drain all lines 
completely by a maintenance man 
who knows the business. If in 
doubt, it is worth the cost to call in 
a good plumber. 

WASHING MACHINES - drain 
and check the hose from the pump. 
Place it downwards in a position so 
that it can be completely emptied. 
Check under trays for any water 
remaining. Again, if in doubt call 
the plumber. 


TOOLS — after inventory, oil all 
tools and wrap in a cloth. Saws 
should be taken to the city or left 
with the local hardware merchant 
for sharpening and storage. If your 
maintenance man lives in the dis¬ 
trict, he will do that work for you. 
DOCKS — get sound advice in this 
area. If they are removable, store 
flat in the lee o’ the land until after 
ice break-up. 

DIVING BOARDS - store flat, in¬ 
doors. Our man suggests oiling be¬ 
fore storing, to keep wood from 
drying out. 

MOTORS AND MOTORBOATS 
—store indoors, preferably protected 
from extreme cold. Motors must be 
drained of gasoline and stored in a 
semi-warm place. A tip from those 
in the Know: drain the motor 
completely, then run the motor un¬ 
til it is dry. 

ROW BOATS AND SAILBOATS 
— should be thoroughly washed out 
in the Fall and dried out before 
storing. 

ROW BOATS - store keels up 
with a piece of 4 X 4 or cord wood 
placed under bow and stern so that 
the boat rests evenly and will not 
warp during storage. 

SAILBOATS — difficulty will occur 
in drying out the bottoms after 
washing. Use a large sponge to 
soak up excess water. Boats should 
then be turned upside down and 
rested evenly on stringers placed at 
the coaming, at the bow and stern. 
Masts should be placed on three 
levelled supports so that they, too, 
will rest evenly to prevent warping. 
CANOES — should be stored keels 
up after being thoroughly cleaned 
and washed inside. Support at bow 
and stern thwarts to prevent warp¬ 
ing. Check for repairs in the fall. 
Repair experts have more time then 
rather than during the Spring rush 
BUILDINGS — where long spans 
occur in any building, temporary 
studs (logs) should be inserted 
between floor and beams to provide 
support against heavy snow loads. 
These can be quickly knocked out 
in the spring. Arrangements should 
be made with local caretaker to 
remove exceptional roof snow loads 
during the winter months. 

THE ROOF — this area should be 
examined in the fall, during every 
rainfall, for possible leaks. Patching 
should be done at marked areas as 
soon as it is dry. Rolled roofing is 
not economical, since it cracks with 


expansion and contraction in tem¬ 
perature changes. Use asbestos 
shingles or metal roofing from the 
outset to save maintenance costs 
each season. 

EAVESTROUGHING - keep a 
constant watch for accumulation of 
leaves and evergreen needles in 
roof gutters and Valleys. They 
should be cleaned regularly to pre¬ 
vent roof leaks. 

CABINS — if cabins . . . and other 
buildings . . . are constructed on 
concrete pads and blocks, they 
should be thoroughly checked each 
spring. Heavy frosts shift the blocks, 
a situation that can twist and tilt 
the structures to a dangerous posi¬ 
tion. 

WINDOWS — cover or camouflage 
them with an old blanket, tarp, can¬ 
vas, even newspaper if necessary. 
Grouse or partridge particularly 
will fly through clear glass and set 
you back the high cost of a new 
window, be it ever so small or large. 
MICKEY MOUSE - like the 
Church Mouse, the Camp Mouse is 
always with us, and knows when to 
take over and conform to his own 
Good Housekeeping standards. 
Mice and squirrels can cause hav- 
ock, and every precaution should be 
taken to discourage their Sit-ins. 
They do not like the strong odours 
of Naphtha Flakes, Spices, Red 
Pepper, Black pepper, Cedar 
branches, Oil of Cedar or Citron- 
ella. Sprinkle these on floors. 
Naphtha Flakes and cedar boughs 
can go on the mattresses. Reserve 
pepper for the floors only. Also 
sprinkle Chloride of Lime powder 
over cabin floors only. Mice won’t 
walk in it. In the Spring, merely 
wash out the cabins with clear hot 
water and you have a good disin¬ 
fectant. 

HINTS FROM DIRECTORS: 
Turn off the cooling unit in the 
walk-in refrigerator. Install an en¬ 
closed heating unit; set it at a 
medium temperature and you have 
an excellent storage area for any¬ 
thing the square footage will 
accommodate. 

NOW, what have we missed? Has 
anyone any questions ... or correc¬ 
tions? If so, send them in to the 
Editor, and add any other sugges¬ 
tions you may dream up. We will 
find answers and include your other 
contributions in the next issue. But 
they must come in pronto!

Dear Mommy & Daddy, 


You told me to drop you a line, so_ I guess 

you don't think that's very funny, but I did and 
so did my new friend Suzie. She's my friend now, 
but she wasn't yesterday because she hurt me. 

It was all her fault; when Miss Smith was showing 
us all how to put a tent up, Suzie was supposed 
to hammer in the wedge for the loop for the tent ropes and the hammer 
hit me in the chin. Dumb Suzie! 



Miss Smith said "Calm Down" just like you say. Mommy. And then we went to the 
Dentist in town. My tooth was broken and had to come out. I can't eat any of the peanut 
brittle you sent; it was yellow anyway. 

Miss Smith says "Don't forget to tell your parents that the camp has Camp-Guard 
and Camp-Guard will take care of the Dentist's bills." 

So that's what I'm doing at camp. I don't like Suzie again because my mouth is still 
sore. 


Love Janie
